name: Delegated Proof of Stake
subject: blockchain
subjectTitle: Blockchain: A Skeptic's Guide to Trust Technologies

lesson.title: Democracy by Committee: Delegated Proof of Stake
lesson.summary: Delegated proof of stake speeds up block production by having token holders elect a small, fixed panel of delegates to validate transactions on everyone's behalf, trading some of proof of stake's decentralization for substantially higher throughput and faster confirmation.
lesson.body:
Proof of stake, as covered in the previous chapter, lets validators earn the right to produce blocks by locking up staked tokens rather than burning electricity. But proof of stake does not by itself specify how many validators should participate or how they should be chosen. If every token holder above some small minimum can independently act as a validator, a network can end up with thousands of participants, and reaching agreement across that many independent parties on every single block takes real coordination time, which limits how fast blocks can be finalized.

Delegated proof of stake, usually abbreviated DPoS, addresses this by having token holders vote, with voting power weighted by how many tokens they hold, to elect a small, fixed set of delegates, sometimes called witnesses or block producers, who actually do the work of validating transactions and producing blocks, typically taking turns in a round robin schedule. The concept was designed by developer Daniel Larimer and first implemented in the BitShares network in 2014. It was later adopted, with variations, by networks including Steem and EOS, the latter of which famously used a panel of twenty one active block producers elected by token holder vote.

The throughput gain comes directly from shrinking and fixing the validator set. Because the block producers are known in advance and few in number, they can hand off block production to each other in a tight, predictable schedule, and reaching agreement among twenty or so known parties takes far less coordination overhead than reaching agreement among thousands of anonymous, geographically scattered validators. Combined with the complete absence of proof of work's computational puzzle, this lets DPoS networks confirm blocks in well under a second in some implementations, and sustain transaction throughput dramatically higher than Bitcoin's roughly seven transactions per second or Ethereum's pre Merge rate in the tens.

That speed is purchased with centralization. Concentrating block production in a small elected panel means a comparatively tiny number of parties control the network's transaction ordering at any given moment, and that panel can be vulnerable to collusion, or to large token holders effectively buying votes by offering to share block rewards with anyone who votes for them. Token holders in principle retain a check on this, since they can vote a misbehaving or underperforming delegate out in the next election cycle, but in practice voter turnout on many DPoS networks has been low, which weakens how strong a check that really is.

DPoS is a clean illustration of the trade off introduced by the scalability trilemma covered next: it is not that DPoS chains found a clever way around the trade off between decentralization and throughput, it is that they made a deliberate choice to sacrifice some decentralization in exchange for speed, a choice that suits some applications, like a fast in game economy, far better than others, like a global reserve asset.
